data.title: Trstín – Nový hrádok, a fortlet revealed by lidar
data.excerpt: Lidar mapping in 2020 and 2021 revealed several previously unknown hillforts in western and central Slovakia, among them a fortlet above Trstín that the Hradiská civic association confirmed in the field in April 2020. The excavation that followed brought a superbly preserved Germanic brooch of the A 45 Almgren type – and 39 lead bullets that finally pinpointed the site of the 1704 battle of Smolenice.

children.text: Lidar mapping in 2020 and 2021 brought the discovery of several new hillforts in both western and central Slovakia. Our civic association Hradiská and its collaborators have of course been following this from the outset and actively search for new hillforts on the basis of the mapping. In April 2020 one of our collaborators – Ladislav Šubovič – drew our attention to a suspicious-looking structure on a hill in the vicinity of Trstín. Shortly afterwards we went to look at the place and were glad to be able to confirm that the hill really is fortified by a small semicircular rampart, and in the enclosure we found several prehistoric sherds. We reported the discovery to the Regional Monuments Board in Trnava, which responded very quickly and ordered an excavation at the fortlet, led by the archaeologist Mgr. Matúš Sládok, PhD., in which we took an active part using a metal detector. The results of our joint survey were summarised by the archaeologist M. Sládok in an extensive text, from which I drew when writing this article.

children.text: The fortification lies on a small promontory with a maximum height of 274 m above sea level above the valley of the Trnávka stream. The promontory is separated by a saddle with a forest track from the mountainous part out of which it projects. The remains of the fortification consist of a low rampart, at most 50 cm high, in the shape of the letter J, which joins the rocky part forming the north-western, western, south-western and partly southern side of the promontory. The fortified area has a maximum length of about 72 m and a maximum width of about 38 m. North-east of this area is a slightly undulating terrain bounded by a linear feature in the shape of the letter U, which could be a bailey. Together, the fortlet and its presumed bailey have a length of about 95 m. Together with the Regional Monuments Board in Trnava we have now placed camera traps at the fortlet in order to document possible illegal metal detectorists.

As for the sherds from vessels, we found seven in all. The pottery is fired both in an oxidising and in a reducing atmosphere. Given the absence of decoration, the sherds are difficult to date. The first group can broadly be assigned to the period from the turn of the Neolithic and the Eneolithic to the Early Iron Age, the second to the same range or to the Roman period, and the third rather to the Roman period or the Early Middle Ages.

Among items of dress and footwear, a brass brooch, two buckles of cast copper alloy and four buttons were found. The superbly preserved Germanic brooch is the most valuable find from the site. It has a coiled spring with a support plate. On the broad bow there are two unclosed eyelets bounded by rings. The bow is decorated with two grooves running parallel to its edges, and in the middle there is a central rib from which a roof-ridged foot with a bevel-cut end extends. Near its heel the foot is decorated with a double incised line in the shape of an inverted letter V. The brooch can be assigned to type A 45 Almgren. We date it to the first half of the 1st century. Some of the buttons, which can be dated to the 17th and 18th centuries, are also worth mentioning. The find of the brooch could be an isolated stray loss, but three sherds datable also to the Roman period were found in the fortified position, and finds similar to one of the finger rings and one of the knives are known from the Roman period as well, which casts the brooch in a different light. In connection with it, two spearheads with facetted sockets found about 1.65 km from the investigated position, north-west of Holbičkov mlyn, dated to the Late La Tène to the Roman period, deserve attention.

Among personal items, three knives, two finger rings of copper alloy and a fire-steel were found. Both finger rings are band-shaped, of sheet metal, with joined ends. The first, ornamental ring is made of thin sheet, without decoration, with a diameter of 17 to 18 mm and a width of 5 mm. Wider band-shaped sheet-metal rings with ends joined by hammering occur at least as early as the Roman period. Band-shaped rings of the 9th to 10th centuries predominantly have unjoined ends.

We found five coins at the hillfort. The oldest coin is a one-sided white penny of Maximilian II from 1566. These were struck in Bohemia as small silver denominations. From the Lesser Carpathians it was contained in two hoards from the territory of Svätý Jur, from the locality known as Dolné Jazvečie. Given their considerable frequency, they held a specific position in monetary affairs and formed part of the everyday payment transactions even of the lowest strata of society. In circulation they probably replaced, or supplemented, the missing small denominations, above all denarii and half-denarii/obols. In addition, their rate against Hungarian coins was easy to calculate, since one Hungarian denarius equalled two Bohemian white pennies. In period documents they appear under the name české babky (Bohemian grannies). Another interesting coin is a silver poltura of Leopold I from 1703. No find of a silver poltura of Leopold I had been known from the Lesser Carpathians.

Surprisingly, the historically most interesting finds proved to be a total of 39 military lead bullets, which can be divided by their shape into three groups – oval projectiles (25 pieces), balls (12 pieces) and a cylinder with two convex sides. Distinct traces on the bullets created by firing, or deformations evidently caused by impact, are visible on 59% of the total number of bullets. Why did these lead balls, which most detectorists throw away as useless rubbish, prove to be important? Because they revealed to us the hitherto unlocated site of an important battle of several centuries ago, of which we have written mentions, but the exact place of the fighting had not been found until our survey. The only military engagement in the Biksárd Pass known from this period is that of 1704, when the so-called battle of Smolenice took place here during the anti-Habsburg estates' uprising of Francis II Rákóczi (1703–1711).

children.text: In it the rebels fought under the command of the generals Miklós Bercsényi, Sándor Károlyi and László Ocskay, reinforced by local armed serfs, against the imperial army led by General Adam Georg Ritschan (Ričán). The imperial troops were camped near Smolenice, and when Ritschan learned that a strong Kuruc army was approaching and that local insurgents were gathering in the area, he decided to withdraw from the camp to Záhorie. The army, together with the family members of some of the officers, left the camp – in which they left fires burning in an attempt to confuse the enemy – at 11 p.m. on 27 May, in a tightly closed column with 70 wagons and 4 cannon as well. At two o'clock in the morning of the following day, when the vanguard reached the forest near Trstín, the column was attacked by Ocskay's units, local serfs and 2,000 of Károlyi's horsemen. The rebels' attacks were indeed repulsed, but in an unfavourable position the imperial troops could not deploy, and in addition the column split into two streams as it advanced. The first part of the first stream, reduced to only about 300 soldiers, emerged from the forest in continuous fighting only at nine o'clock in the morning, and reached Jablonica around five in the afternoon. The second part of this stream, likewise constantly attacked by the rebels, also emerged from the forest, greatly thinned out, around one in the afternoon. The remnants of the imperial troops gathered at the manor house in Jablonica and in its surroundings, and before long they were surrounded by the rebels. Ritschan, wounded in the fighting in the pass, at first tried to fortify himself provisionally, but in the end his officers persuaded him to surrender in a hopeless situation against overwhelming odds. Only the cavalry unit of Captain Giordani managed to escape from Jablonica. The second stream, under the command of Colonel Wachtendonk, which had lost contact with the first in the hills, managed to withdraw past Korlátka Castle and Plavecký Castle towards Austria, where 1,100 soldiers arrived. For the clash at the beginning of the battle Wachtendonk gives losses of 100 imperial and 300 Kuruc soldiers. The total imperial losses in the battle are given very differently – from 300–400 to almost 4,000 killed, about 700 to about 2,000 (horsemen) captured, and one to all of the cannon. The total number of Kuruc dead is not known.

children.text: We therefore connect the lead bullets with the battle of Smolenice described above. The fortlet itself lies only about 650 m from what was originally one of the two main roads through the Biksárd Pass. The nearest bullet was found only about 600 m from it. Directly below the fortlet a road runs along the valley of the Trnávka stream, through which, according to J. Bánlaky, the imperial army withdrew laboriously across marshy terrain, but according to the map of the same researcher they withdrew along the above-mentioned historical main road. According to this map the local insurgents occupied the pass from the valley of the Trnávka, across the above-mentioned nearby main route, as far as the left side of the valley of the Raková stream, through which main road no. 51 runs today – that is, including the area of the site. The bullets do not come from anti-personnel artillery, since for reasons of effectiveness it was used only in unwooded, predominantly flatter terrain, against masses of opponents, and there are no mentions of its use in this battle either. The oval projectiles can be assigned with certainty to pistols. Their shape arose from the hammering out of balls intended for weapons of larger calibre (carbines, arquebuses or a light musket). The hammering out is proved by the flat facets on the projectiles created by hammer blows on the balls. Of the balls, some are from pistols, but the majority may also be from carbines, arquebuses or light muskets. The overall predominance of bullets from cavalry weapons, if not their entire number, proves a clash here between a cavalry unit and infantry, or a clash of two cavalry units. In the present state of investigation of part of the battlefield we believe that the imperial cavalry probably drove back the local insurgents here as they attacked the retreating column. The find of the rare coin issue of 1703 mentioned above is probably also connected with the battle in the pass. It would be very bold to link some of the other finds, for example the knives, buttons, a horseshoe and nails, with the battle, because they are not precisely datable or may also relate to other activities. The significance of our discovery lies above all in the fact that it is the first battle of the period of the estates' uprisings in Slovakia to be documented by relevant archaeological finds outside the siege and capture of fortifications.

children.text: It was not possible to date when the rampart fortification itself was built, but we rule out its origin in the High Middle Ages or the modern period, since fortifications of that time are typically more massive and of a different shape, since at fortifications of the High and Late Middle Ages finds of militaria, nails and pottery are frequent, and since in the modern period the main roads through the pass did not run below the fortlet, so a fortification here would have made no sense. The sherds can be dated to a broad period from the turn of the Neolithic and the Eneolithic up to the Early Middle Ages, with the exception of the La Tène period, and within this range we identified at least two periods – the Eneolithic to the Hallstatt period, and the Roman period or the Early Middle Ages. The handful of sherds testifies to only short-term stays at the position (a place of refuge?). Such inconspicuous fortifications are not typical of the Bronze Age, the Hallstatt period or the Early Middle Ages, and from the Roman period we do not know of them in Germanic territory within the territory of present-day Slovakia. From the Eneolithic we do know of slight fortifications in the Lesser Carpathians. At Prašník, in the locality known as Hrádok, a palisade trench dated to the Ludanice group of the Lengyel culture was identified.
